highlights.title: China promised less CO₂ per unit of economic output
highlights.body: In 2015, China pledged to cut CO₂ intensity by 60–65% from 2005 levels by 2030, and peak emissions around 2030. The later target of 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity was reached in 2024. That meets a partial target; the original overall pledge still requires separate assessment.
highlights.stat_label: The 2030 wind/solar target was reached in 2024

highlights.kicker: India · A target benchmark reached early
highlights.title: India passed its original emissions intensity benchmark well ahead
highlights.body: India pledged in 2015 to reduce greenhouse gases per unit of GDP by 33–35% from 2005 levels by 2030. The government reported a 37.38% reduction for 2022, already beyond the original benchmark. Falling intensity can still accompany rising total emissions in a growing economy; the other pledges require separate assessment.

highlights.kicker: Türkiye · Reduction relative to a scenario
highlights.title: Türkiye promised less than a projected growth scenario
highlights.body: The 2015 pledge was up to 21% below business-as-usual emissions by 2030. EDGAR estimates emissions excluding land use rose from 464.73 million tonnes in 2015 to 610.78 million in 2025. This increase of about 31.4% does not, by itself, establish failure to meet the differently defined BAU target.

highlights.title: Saudi Arabia’s first pledge also depended on oil exports
highlights.body: Saudi Arabia’s 2015 pledge offered annual avoidance of up to 130 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent against a dynamic baseline by 2030. Conditions included growth and diversification with robust oil export revenues. EDGAR estimates 2025 emissions excluding land use at 844.96 million tonnes. That figure alone cannot show the promised avoidance relative to the scenario.

highlights.title: Germany’s progress does not establish fulfilment of the EU target
highlights.body: Germany began with the joint EU pledge: at least 40% below 1990 greenhouse gases by 2030. Its national emissions were 48.2% below 1990 in 2025; that does not establish fulfilment of the shared EU target. For Germany’s current 65% reduction target for 2030, the environment agency’s 2026 projection shows only 62.6%.
highlights.stat_label: Germany in 2025 relative to 1990, excluding land use

highlights.kicker: Brazil · Forest protection and the overall balance
highlights.title: Less deforestation does not settle the entire climate pledge
highlights.body: Brazil pledged in 2015 to cut greenhouse gases by 37% from 2005 levels by 2025. Forest protection shows progress: INPE measured 41.8% less Amazon deforestation from August 2025 to July 2026 than in the previous year. This partial indicator does not establish complete fulfilment of the original economy-wide 2025 target.
highlights.stat_label: Amazon deforestation area in 2025/26 versus the previous year

highlights.kicker: Timor-Leste · Explicitly declining a numerical target
highlights.title: Timor-Leste explicitly chose not to set a quantified emissions target
highlights.body: In its October 2016 contribution, Timor-Leste explicitly chose not to set an emissions reduction target. It still proposed measures in transport, agriculture, forestry and energy, requiring international climate finance and help to build an economy-wide greenhouse gas inventory. There is no reduction percentage here, but measures and support needs are documented.
highlights.stat_label: Contribution without a quantified emissions reduction target

highlights.title: Falling gross emissions do not guarantee a falling net total
highlights.body: South Korea pledged in 2015 to cut 2030 emissions by 37% against a BAU level of 850.6 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent. Its provisional inventory shows gross emissions fell 0.9% in 2025, while net emissions including land use rose 0.5%, partly because of forest fires. Comparison with the original target requires consistent inventory methods.

de.title: Deutschland: weniger Emissionen, kaum Wachstum
de.intro: Deutschlands reales BIP lag 2025 rund 7,6 % über dem Wert von 2015. Das entspricht im geometrischen Jahresdurchschnitt nur 0,74 % Wachstum. Die Zehnjahreszahl verdeckt die jüngste Stagnation.
body: Im selben Jahrzehnt sanken die erfassten Treibhausgasemissionen um 26,8 %. Ein späterer Ausgangspunkt verändert das Wirtschaftsbild deutlich: Von 2019 bis 2025 wuchs das reale BIP insgesamt nur um 0,3 %, während die Emissionen um 17,8 % sanken. Von 2022 bis 2025 schrumpfte die Wirtschaftsleistung um 1,1 %; der Ausstoß ging um 12,4 % zurück. Alle Angaben vergleichen jeweils dieselben Anfangs- und Endjahre.

2015, 2019 und 2022 sind Vergleichsjahre, keine nachgewiesenen Startpunkte der Wirkung einzelner Klimamaßnahmen. Der längste Zeitraum beginnt im Paris-Jahr; die kürzeren Fenster machen die jüngste wirtschaftliche Schwäche sichtbar. Sie überlappen sich und dürfen nicht addiert werden.

Reales BIP ist bereits um Preisänderungen bereinigt. Die Inflation davon nochmals abzuziehen wäre eine doppelte Korrektur. Zugleich ist eine sinkende Inflationsrate kein sinkendes Preisniveau: Solange die Rate positiv bleibt, steigen die Preise weiter, nur langsamer. Das gesamtwirtschaftliche BIP zeigt außerdem nicht, wie sich Kaufkraft und Lebenshaltungskosten einzelner Haushalte entwickelt haben.

Die Schwäche hat mehrere nachgewiesene Begleiterscheinungen. Destatis berichtete im Januar 2026 über rückläufige Exporte und Investitionen sowie schwache Industrie- und Bauaktivität. Das UBA verbindet einen Teil des industriellen Emissionsrückgangs 2025 mit geringerer Produktion. Eine IMF-Arbeitsstudie vom Juni 2026 untersucht sowohl Konjunktur als auch Produktivität, Investitionsmängel, Demografie und den Energiepreisschock von 2022.

Aus dieser Gegenüberstellung lässt sich der Anteil der Klimapolitik an Wachstum oder Emissionsrückgang nicht bestimmen. Dafür müssten unter anderem Energiepreise, Branchenstruktur, Nachfrage und Produktionsverlagerungen getrennt untersucht werden. Deutschlands jüngste Entwicklung verlangt deshalb eine Einordnung von wirtschaftlicher Schwäche und technischer Emissionsminderung.

Die Prozentwerte wurden aus der Weltbank-Reihe zum realen BIP und EDGAR-Emissionen berechnet, Datenstand November 2026. EDGAR erfasst hier territoriale Treibhausgase ohne Landnutzung und Forstwirtschaft; importierte Emissionen bleiben außen vor. Die ergänzende UBA-Quelle verwendet das nationale Inventar und ist eine separate Einordnung.

en.title: Germany: lower emissions, little growth
en.intro: Germany’s real GDP in 2025 was about 7.6% above its 2015 level. That amounts to a compound annual growth rate of just 0.74%. The decade-wide figure conceals the recent stagnation.
body: Recorded greenhouse gas emissions fell by 26.8% over the same decade. A later starting point changes the economic picture markedly: between 2019 and 2025, real GDP grew by just 0.3% in total, while emissions fell by 17.8%. From 2022 to 2025, economic output contracted by 1.1%; emissions declined by 12.4%. Each comparison uses matching start and end years.

2015, 2019 and 2022 are comparison years, not established dates when particular climate policies began taking effect. The longest period starts in the Paris year; the shorter windows reveal the recent economic weakness. These periods overlap and cannot be added together.

Real GDP already adjusts for price changes. Subtracting inflation again would make the same correction twice. A falling inflation rate also does not mean a falling price level: while the rate remains positive, prices continue rising, just more slowly. Aggregate GDP does not show how individual households’ purchasing power and living costs have changed.

Several documented developments accompany the weakness. In January 2026, Destatis reported declining exports and investment, alongside weak manufacturing and construction. Germany’s environment agency, UBA, links part of the industrial emissions decline in 2025 to lower production. An IMF working paper published in June 2026 examines cyclical conditions alongside productivity, underinvestment, demographics and the 2022 energy-price shock.

This comparison cannot establish climate policy’s contribution to growth or emissions reductions. That requires examining energy prices, the composition of industry, demand and production relocation separately. Germany’s recent performance therefore calls for assessing both economic weakness and technical emissions reductions.

The percentages were calculated from World Bank real GDP and EDGAR emissions series, using data available in November 2026. Here, EDGAR measures territorial greenhouse gases excluding land use and forestry; emissions embodied in imports are outside the measure. The supplementary UBA source uses Germany’s national inventory and provides separate context.
